title: Heat, air pollution, and global temperature shocks
gist: A World Bank economist reviews new work by Bilal and Känzig using global temperature shocks which finds a permanent 1°C warming raises mortality by 2.5 deaths per 1,000 people annually, 1-2 orders of magnitude above local-heat estimates, mostly via a 22% long-run fall in world GDP per capita, undermining the case for prioritizing air pollution over climate in developing countries.

insights.claim: Some argue low- and middle-income countries should prioritize air pollution over climate because pollution imposes large mortality and economic costs now while climate damages arrive mostly at the end of the century.
insights.so_what: Frames the policy trade-off driving where development and green capital flows.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Historical estimates put heat mortality in 2050 at roughly 0.03-0.04 deaths per 1,000 people per year under moderate warming, versus current air-pollution mortality of 0.8-1.2 per 1,000 and about 1.6 per 1,000 in India.
insights.so_what: Under conventional estimates, air pollution dominates environmental mortality through mid-century.
insights.quote: Mortality from air pollution today is somewhere between 0.8 and 1.2 deaths per 1,000 people per year.
insights.locator: The case for air pollution first
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Under conventional local-shock estimates, air-pollution mortality in 2050 would still be about five times heat mortality even with substantial air-quality improvements, with the two becoming comparable only around 2100.
insights.so_what: Explains why many LMIC policymakers have historically favored pollution control.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Some policies, such as reducing coal-fired power generation, address both air pollution and climate change at once, but such win-win solutions do not always exist.
insights.so_what: Coal phase-down has double policy support, strengthening its political durability.
insights.quote: Some policies address both problems at once (reducing coal-fired power generation, for example). But win-win solutions do not always exist.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Most climate-impact estimates come from localized weather shocks, effectively measuring partial equilibrium effects, whereas climate change raises temperatures in many places at once and is a general equilibrium problem.
insights.so_what: Standard climate-damage models used in risk pricing may systematically understate impacts.
insights.quote: much of the existing empirical literature estimates a partial equilibrium effect, while the impact of climate change is a general equilibrium question.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Adrien Bilal and Diego Känzig identify climate impacts using global deviations from expected temperature driven by natural variability such as El Niño, solar cycles and volcanic eruptions, which are exogenous to local conditions.
insights.so_what: Novel identification strategy yields much larger damage estimates, with implications for climate-risk models.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Bilal and Känzig estimate a permanent 1°C rise in global temperature raises annual mortality by 2.5 deaths per 1,000 people, versus 0.1 per 1,000 from local heat exposure alone.
insights.so_what: If correct, climate mortality costs are 1-2 orders of magnitude larger than assumed, raising the social cost of carbon.
insights.quote: a permanent 1°C increase in global temperature raises annual mortality by 2.5 deaths per 1,000 people, compared to 0.1 per 1,000 from local heat exposure alone
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The new estimates imply that by 2050 mortality from warming will exceed present air-pollution mortality, with impacts in Africa, Asia and Latin America substantially larger than the global average.
insights.so_what: Emerging-market regions face disproportionate climate-driven human and economic losses.
insights.quote: The impacts in Africa, Asia, and Latin America will be substantially larger than the global average.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Bilal and Känzig's earlier work estimates a permanent 1°C rise in global temperature lowers world GDP per capita by 22% in the long run, and this income decline explains most of warming's mortality effect.
insights.so_what: Implies very large macro damages from warming, far above standard IAM assumptions.
insights.quote: a permanent 1°C rise in global temperature lowers world GDP per capita by 22% in the long run.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The results suggest substantial mortality from warming already exists today, so climate adaptation would likely deliver immediate rather than only distant benefits.
insights.so_what: Strengthens near-term demand for adaptation spending (cooling, health, resilient infrastructure).
insights.quote: actions to reduce the future damages of climate change will likely have immediate benefits, which further strengthens the case for climate adaptation.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The article notes the world is currently going through a particularly strong El Niño that is pushing global temperatures up.
insights.so_what: Strong El Niño raises near-term risk to agriculture, commodities and heat-sensitive sectors.
insights.quote: We’re currently going through a particularly strong El Niño, which is pushing global temperatures up.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The global-shock approach relies on a single global time series with a small sample and no year fixed effects, so unobserved global shocks coinciding with temperature shocks could contaminate the estimates.
insights.so_what: The headline damage numbers carry significant model uncertainty.
insights.quote: any unobserved global shock that happens to coincide with a temperature shock is not averaged out.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The author cautions against deprioritizing air pollution on the basis of one study, since projected 2050 pollution reductions will only materialize if pollution gets attention and resources today.
insights.so_what: Pollution-control spending in LMICs should continue alongside climate adaptation.
insights.quote: This is not an argument for prioritizing climate adaptation at the expense of work on air pollution on the basis of a single study.
insights.locator: What this does and does not change
insights.speaker: @worldbank
